top_choice_rationale: P002 (Kiyotaki and Moore) rewards one foundational mechanism: borrowing limits tied to collateral values link asset prices and credit, so temporary shocks become large, persistent and propagated across sectors. The originator attribution is as clean as any on the slate, since the 1997 paper is the origin and its two authors are its originators. The work is nearly thirty years old and has been extended, quantified and applied. A citation on collateral constraints and credit cycles can be kept distinct from the 2022 prize on banks, runs and intermediation, and leaving out Gertler and Gilchrist rests on that scope. P001 (Autor, Hanson, Katz) is scientifically very strong, with broad and directly tested empirical evidence, and it is my clear second choice. Its cost is attribution: it excludes Dorn, and it joins a skills-and-technology strand with a trade-shock strand that some members read as two achievements. Tested empirical confirmation counts for P001, and the attribution argument counts for P002. I rank P002 first on attribution and maturity, not on how many members support either proposal. No award is ranked last because both proposals describe mature, defensible achievements.
recusal_note: No connection to the credited names in P001 (Autor, Hanson, Katz) or P002 (Kiyotaki, Moore) is apparent from my profile. Disclosed ties are to committee members, not candidates: I co-authored with Boppart and Friberg and frequently with Krusell (secretary), and I am an IIES colleague of Krusell and Boppart. The 2018 Scientific Background cites my own work, and whether I drafted any of it is undocumented. I am a macroeconomist, which may bias me toward a macro-finance candidate. Conflicts are disclosed, not adjudicated, and I have completed the ballot.
